name: New study shows steroids can save lives of preterm babies

content.title: New study shows steroids can save lives of preterm babies
content.summary: AKU researchers in Pakistan were part of the multi-country trial in low-income countries.

media.alt: New study shows steroids can save lives of preterm babies

content.text: A package of interventions that includes giving the steroid dexamethasone to pregnant women at high risk of preterm birth can help save babies' lives, according to a study in
The New England Journal of Medicine
, NEJM, the most prestigious and highly cited medical journal in the world.

AKU researchers, Drs Shabina Ariff and Sajid Soofi, associate professor and professor, respectively, in AKU Medical College's department of paediatrics and child health and Dr Lumaan Sheikh, chairperson of the department of obstetrics and gynaecology, were part of the multi-country randomised trial, World Health Organization ACTION-I (Antenatal Corticosteroids for Improving Outcomes in Preterm Newborns), which assessed the safety and efficacy of dexamethasone in low-resource countries such as Bangladesh, India, Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan.

Preterm birth is the leading cause of death in children under the age of five, according to the World Health Organization, WHO. This is because babies who are born too early - before 37 weeks of age - often have underdeveloped lungs. This leads to them suffering from a breathing disorder, respiratory distress syndrome or RDS that is one of the top causes of death and disability among preterm newborns.

The trial found that one premature baby's life was saved for every 25 pregnant women treated with dexamethasone. This is because the drug helps accelerate lung development thereby reducing the chance and severity of the baby having respiratory problems such as RDS at birth. The study also noted that dexamethasone significantly lowers the risk of neonatal death and stillbirth and that the drug does not increase the likelihood of the mother contracting an infection during pregnancy.

"When a minimal package of care for newborn babies - including management of infection, feeding support, thermal care and access to a CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure, machine to support respiration - is in place in low-income countries, antenatal steroids such as dexamethasone can help to save preterm babies' lives," says Dr Rajiv Bahl, head of the newborn health unit at WHO and one of the study coordinators.
The study also found that the drug is most effective when administered 48 hours before giving birth and noted that it was most likely to be of use between the 26th and 34th weeks of pregnancy.

While dexamethasone and similar drugs have long shown to be effective in saving preterm babies living in high-income countries, the WHO Action-I study provides the first evidence of the value of the drugs in low-income settings.
The objectives of the trial are in line with global efforts under the UN Sustainable Development Goal 3 to end preventable deaths of newborns and children under the age of 5.
The trial was conducted between December 2017 and November 2019 and recruited 2,852 women and their 3,070 babies from 29 secondary and tertiary level hospitals in the five countries.
